slides.title:
The two pages
that lose the deal.
slides.sub:
11 pages: the average winner.
13 pages: the average loser.

text: Nobody adds two pages on purpose. They arrive one worried paragraph at a time. Proposify looked at 742,137 proposals sent in 2025: the average winner ran 11 pages, the average loser 13. Before you send, find the two pages you wrote for yourself.

slides.title:
Two sections do
two-thirds of the work.

text: You spent a week on the process section. They spent a minute. Better Proposals measured where reading time goes: 38.2% on the introduction, 27% on pricing, 34.8% on everything else combined. Write the first page and the price page first, and last, and best.

slides.title:
Out of every hundred invoices,
twenty-nine are still waiting.
slides.sub: Most of them arrive within two weeks of the due date.

text: The work is done. The invoice is sent. And then the waiting starts. Bonsai analysed three years of freelance invoices: 29% were paid at least a day late. The same data says most arrive within two weeks of the due date. One polite reminder on day one does more than a stern one on day thirty.

slides.title:
They read the ones
they sign for longer.

text: A yes takes time. Buyers spent 25.3 minutes on the proposals they signed and 15.8 on the ones they turned down, across 742,137 proposals in Proposify's data. Reading time is the closest thing to a heartbeat a proposal has. On a Recto link you can see it, page by page.

slides.title:
Seventeen minutes to make.
Two and a half days to decide.

text: The average proposal took 17 minutes to make. The buyer opened it 34 minutes after it was sent, and closed the deal two and a half days after opening it (Proposify, 2026). The decision is quick. The document that decides months of work deserves more than a lunch break.

slides.title:
Paper means a meeting
you're not in.

text: Somewhere a proposal is being passed around a table, annotated in someone else's pen. Better Proposals found that when a client prints your proposal, you're 84% less likely to win. You can't stop the printer. You can make page one speak for you when you're not there.

slides.title:
The bigger the invoice,
the longer the wait.

text: Small invoices get paid between meetings. Big ones need a signature, a budget line and someone back from holiday. Bonsai found invoices over $20,000 were three times more likely to be paid late than invoices under $100. On a big project, split the money: a deposit, then milestones.

slides.quote:
This sentence is set
in Baskerville.
Did you believe it
a little more?
slides.sub:
In a 2012 test of about 45,000 New York Times readers,
Errol Morris found Baskerville drew the most agreement
of six typefaces. Not a lab study, and he said so.

text: In 2012 Errol Morris showed the same passage to about 45,000 New York Times readers in six typefaces. Baskerville drew the most agreement and the least disagreement. The effect was small and the test wasn't a lab study. But type speaks before the words do. Choose it like you mean it.

slides.title:
Eleven to win it.
Eighteen to keep it.

text: Agencies in the ANA and 4A's study put an average of 11 people on a new-business pitch, and 18 when they were defending an existing account. Seven extra people, all of them not working on anything else. Before the next yes, count the chairs, not just the hours.

slides.title:
Defending costs
twice what attacking does.

text: ANA and the 4A's put the average cost of a pitch at $406,092 for the incumbent agency and $204,461 for an outsider. Defending is the expensive side. The cheapest pitch is the one you never have to make, because the relationship never went cold.

slides.title:
More choice.
Fewer yeses.

text: The bigger table drew more shoppers. The smaller one sold more jam. In Iyengar and Lepper's study, 3% bought from 24 options and 30% from 6. Later research argues about how far the effect goes, but every studio knows the feeling of a client lost between seven packages. Offer three.

slides.title:
The slow proposal
gets the slow yes.

text: The meeting went well. Everyone was excited. Then the proposal took four days. Better Proposals found proposals sent within 24 hours were signed in about 6 days, and those sent three or four days later took almost 12. Excitement has a shelf life. Send while it's fresh.

slides.title:
They say they buy ideas.
Then they read the price.

text: Clients in ANA and 4A's research named cost and price as the top factor in choosing an agency (62%), well ahead of creative execution (45%), the big idea (36%) and reputation (35%). The work gets you shortlisted. A clear, confident price page gets you picked.

slides.title:
Most of us have chased
money we already earned.
slides.sub:
of freelancers have had trouble getting paid
at some point. Freelancers Union surveyed 5,358.

text: If it has happened to you, you're in the majority. Freelancers Union surveyed 5,358 freelancers: 71% had trouble getting paid at some point in their career. It isn't a sign you're bad at business. It's a sign the paperwork has to do more of the work: deposits, due dates, terms in writing.

slides.title:
Most late invoices
aren't refused. They're forgotten.

text: Bonsai found 90% of late invoices were paid within a month of the due date, and over 75% within two weeks. Late usually means buried, not refused. A Recto invoice moves from draft to sent, viewed, overdue and paid, so you know whether it was opened before you send the nudge.

slides.title:
Sign it
before they do.

text: An unsigned proposal reads like a draft. A signed one reads like an offer. In Proposify's data, proposals the sender signed before sending had a 65% higher close rate and closed 25% faster. Put your name on it first. A Recto document ends with a signature block for exactly that.

slides.title:
Seven sections.
No more.

text: Two different studies, the same number. Better Proposals found its best-converting proposals averaged 7 sections, and Proposify's 2026 data says the same about winning proposals. Which seven is your call. This is ours: problem, approach, scope, timeline, proof, price, next step.

slides.title:
Winners get read
twelve times.
slides.sub:
Winning proposals were opened 12 times on average.
Losing ones, 8.

text: Nobody reads a proposal twelve times for fun. They read it, forward it, defend it in a meeting and read it again before signing. Proposify found winning proposals were viewed 12 times on average, losing ones 8. Every one of those views is someone deciding. Make page one easy to defend.

slides.title:
Your words
still matter.
slides.sub:
Albert Mehrabian's 1967 experiments tested single words carrying
feelings. He has said they don't apply to everyday communication.

text: You've seen the slide: 7% words, 38% voice, 55% body language. It comes from Albert Mehrabian's 1967 experiments on single words carrying feelings, and Mehrabian has said it doesn't apply to everyday communication. Presenters, your words matter. Write them like they do.

slides.title:
A working month a year,
spent asking to be paid.
slides.sub: About 20 working days a year chasing late payments.

text: UK research by IPSE found freelancers spend about 20 days a year chasing late payments. That's a whole working month of emails that start with 'Just following up'. Put the deposit, the due date and the late terms in the proposal, so the chasing starts before anyone is late.

slides.title:
Same work.
Different wait.
slides.sub:
Share of invoices paid late, controlling for skills,
experience and client size.

text: In Bonsai's invoice data, 31% of invoices from women freelancers were paid late, against 24% for men and 23% for studios, even after controlling for skills, experience and client size. Worth knowing. Worth saying out loud. Worth sharing with the client who pays everyone late.

slides.title:
You designed for A4.
They met it on a phone.

text: You set it on A4 with perfect margins. They opened it in a taxi. Better Proposals found 37.7% of proposals were first opened on a phone. A Recto link opens as plain slides, a page-turning book or a magazine spread, so the first look doesn't have to be a pinch and a zoom.

slides.title: Price the after.

text: Launch day isn't the end of the work, so it shouldn't be the end of the price. Better Proposals found offers with monthly fees sold for 28.5% more, against 16.3% for offers with only initial costs. If you'll be there after launch, put the after in the proposal.

slides.title:
Seven is a myth.
Four is a plan.

text: George Miller's 'magical number seven' is quoted on every presentation course. Later research by Nelson Cowan put working memory closer to four chunks. Four packages. Four steps. Four numbers on a slide. After that, people stop holding and start skimming.

slides.title:
Change a quantity at midnight.
The total is right by morning.
slides.sub: Rows multiply and total themselves as you type.
